code: ### Empirical 401(k) Examples  data("fracreg_k401k")  y <- fracreg_k401k$prate  X <- cbind(mrate = fracreg_k401k$mrate, age = fracreg_k401k$age,              totemp = fracreg_k401k$totemp, sole = fracreg_k401k$sole)    # 1P Model  fracreg(y, X, type="1P", linkfrac="logit")    # 2P Model (modelling mass at 1)  fracreg(y, X, type="2P", inflation=1, linkbin="logit", linkfrac="logit")    # 3P Model (inject artificial 0s for demonstration)  y_3p <- y; y_3p[1:50] <- 0  fracreg(y_3p, X, type="3P", linkbin=c("logit","logit"), linkfrac="logit")    ### Simulated Examples    set.seed(123)  N <- 1000  x1 <- rnorm(N)  x2 <- runif(N)    # Generating a fractional dependent variable with inflation at 0 and 1  XB <- -0.5 + 0.8 * x1 + 1.2 * x2 + rnorm(N)  y_latent <- exp(XB) / (1 + exp(XB))    y <- y_latent  # Inflate at boundaries  y[y_latent < 0.2] <- 0  y[y_latent > 0.8] <- 1    X <- cbind(x1 = x1, x2 = x2)    # fracreg estimation of a logit fractional response model  fracreg(y, X, type="1P", linkfrac="logit")    # fracreg estimation of the binary logit component of the two-part fractional  # regression model with y=0 as the relevant boundary value  fracreg(y, X, type="2Pbin", inflation=0, linkbin="logit")    # fracreg estimation of the fractional component of the two-part fractional  # regression model with y=0 as the relevant boundary value and using a  # probit link function  fracreg(y, X, type="2Pfrac", inflation=0, linkfrac="probit")    # fracreg estimation of both components of a two-part fractional response model  # with y=0 as the relevant boundary value and using a cloglog binary link  # function and a logit fractional link function  fracreg(y, X, type="2P", inflation=0, linkbin="cloglog", linkfrac="logit")    # Three-part double-inflated model (y has both 0s and 1s)  fracreg(y, X, type="3P", linkbin=c("logit","probit"), linkfrac="logit")

code: ### Empirical 401(k) Examples  data("fracreg_k401k")  y <- fracreg_k401k$prate  X <- cbind(mrate = fracreg_k401k$mrate, age = fracreg_k401k$age,              totemp = fracreg_k401k$totemp, sole = fracreg_k401k$sole)    # Artificial instrumental variable for demonstration  Z_emp <- cbind(X, z = fracreg_k401k$mrate * rnorm(length(y)))  fracreghet(y, X, Z_emp, var.endog = X[, "mrate"], type="QMLxv", link="logit")    ### Simulated Examples    set.seed(123)  N <- 1000  x1 <- rnorm(N)    # Simulating an endogenous variable (var.endog) and an instrument (z1)  z1 <- rnorm(N)  u <- 0.5 * z1 + rnorm(N)  var.endog <- 0.8 * z1 + u  y_endog <- exp(0.5 * x1 + 1.2 * var.endog + u) / (1 + exp(0.5 * x1 + 1.2 * var.endog + u))    # Avoid exact 0 or 1 boundaries for some estimators  y_endog[y_endog <= 0] <- 0.01  y_endog[y_endog >= 1] <- 0.99    X <- cbind(x1 = x1, var.endog = var.endog)  Z <- cbind(x1 = x1, z1 = z1)    # Exogeneity (assuming var.endog is exogenous for comparison), GMMx estimator  fracreghet(y = y_endog, x = X, type = "GMMx", link = "logit")    # Endogeneity, GMMz estimator (does not require reduced form for endog)  fracreghet(y = y_endog, x = X, z = Z, type = "GMMz", link = "logit")    # Endogeneity, GMMxv estimator (assumes linear reduced form for var.endog)  fracreghet(y = y_endog, x = X, z = Z, var.endog = var.endog, type = "GMMxv", link = "logit")    # Endogeneity, QMLxv control function approach  fracreghet(y = y_endog, x = X, z = Z, var.endog = var.endog, type = "QMLxv", link = "logit")

code: ### Empirical 401(k) Examples  data("fracreg_k401k")  y <- fracreg_k401k$prate  X <- cbind(mrate = fracreg_k401k$mrate, age = fracreg_k401k$age,              totemp = fracreg_k401k$totemp, sole = fracreg_k401k$sole)    # Artificial panel data structure for demonstration  N_emp <- nrow(X)  id_emp <- rep(1:(N_emp/2), each=2)  time_emp <- rep(1:2, times=N_emp/2)  fracregpd(id_emp, time_emp, y, X, type="QMLcre", link="probit")    ### Simulated Examples    set.seed(123)  # Simulating Panel Data  N <- 100  T_periods <- 5  id <- rep(1:N, each = T_periods)  time <- rep(1:T_periods, times = N)  x_panel <- rnorm(N * T_periods)    # Unobserved individual effect (CRE)  c_i <- rep(rnorm(N), each = T_periods)   y_panel <- exp(x_panel + c_i) / (1 + exp(x_panel + c_i))    X <- cbind(x_panel = x_panel)    # Endogenous variable and instrument simulation  z_panel <- rnorm(N * T_periods)  u_panel <- 0.5 * z_panel + rnorm(N * T_periods)  var_endog <- 0.8 * z_panel + u_panel  y_endog <- exp(x_panel + 1.2 * var_endog + c_i + u_panel) /                (1 + exp(x_panel + 1.2 * var_endog + c_i + u_panel))    X_endog <- cbind(x_panel = x_panel, var_endog = var_endog)  Z_inst <- cbind(x_panel = x_panel, z_panel = z_panel)    # Estimate a Correlated Random Effects (CRE) Model  fracregpd(id=id, time=time, y=y_panel, x=X, type="QMLcre", link="probit")    # Exogeneity, no lags, no time dummies, clustered standard errors, GMMbgw estimator  fracregpd(id=id, time=time, y=y_panel, x=X, type="GMMbgw")    # Lagged covariates and instruments, robust standard errors, GMMww estimator  fracregpd(id=id, time=time, y=y_panel, x=X, lags=TRUE, type="GMMww", var.type="robust")    # Endogeneity, time dummies, GMMpfe estimator  fracregpd(id=id, time=time, y=y_endog, x=X_endog, z=Z_inst,             x.exogenous=FALSE, type="GMMpfe", tdummies=TRUE)

title: Fitting Fractional Response Regressions — fracreg
text: fracreg estimates one-part, two-part hurdle, three-part double-inflated fractional response models; see Ramalho, Ramalho Murteira (2011) Fang Ma (2013) details models. One-Part Fractional Response Regressions (type = "1P"): standard one-part model assumes conditional expectation fractional response \(y_i \[0,1]\) given : $$E(y_i|x_i) = G(x_i \beta)$$ \(G(\cdot)\) known non-linear link function mapping linear predictor unit interval (e.g., logit, probit). parameters \(\beta\) estimated maximising Bernoulli-based quasi-log-likelihood function: $$\ln L_i(\beta) = y_i \ln[G(x_i \beta)] + (1 - y_i) \ln[1 - G(x_i \beta)]$$ estimator requires correct specification conditional mean yield consistent parameter estimates (Papke Wooldridge, 1996). Two-Part Hurdle Models (type = "2P"): data exhibits boundary mass (e.g., \(y_i = 0\)), two-part hurdle model handles boundary values separately interior fractional values. Let \(y_i^*\) binary indicator \(y_i^* = 1\) \(y_i > 0\) \(y_i^* = 0\) otherwise. probability observing boundary value modelled : $$P(y_i = 0 | x_{1i}) = 1 - F(x_{1i} \gamma_1)$$ $$P(y_i > 0 | x_{1i}) = F(x_{1i} \gamma_1)$$ \(F(\cdot)\) binary link function. Conditional observing interior fractional value, response modelled : $$E(y_i | x_{2i}, y_i > 0) = G(x_{2i} \beta_2)$$ unconditional mean response therefore: $$E(y_i|x_i) = F(x_{1i} \gamma_1) \times G(x_{2i} \beta_2)$$ Three-Part Double Inflated Models (type = "3P"): data containing boundary mass \(0\) \(1\), three-part model estimates two separate binary mechanisms boundary fractional component interior values \((0, 1)\), extending two-part logic double inflation (Fang Ma, 2013). fracreg uses standard glm command perform estimations. Therefore, fracreg essentially convenience command, allowing estimation several alternative fractional response models using command. addition, fracreg provides R-squared measure models (calculated square correlation coefficient actual fitted values dependent variable), calculates fitted values dependent variable two-part models stores information needed implement useful commands fractional response models: fracreg.reset (RESET test), fracreg.ptest (P test), fracreg.ggoff (GGOFF tests) fracreg.pe (partial effects).

text: fracreg.pe calculates partial effects fractional response models estimated via fracreg. fracreg.pe may used compute average conditional partial effects : () one-part fractional response models; (ii) binary components two-part three-part fractional response models; (iii) fractional components two-part three-part fractional response models; (iv) two-part three-part fractional response models overall. Partial Effects Continuous Variables: continuous covariate \(x_k\), partial effect conditional mean \(E(y|x) = G(x\beta)\) first derivative respect \(x_k\): $$PE_k(x) = \frac{\partial E(y|x)}{\partial x_k} = g(x\beta)\beta_k$$ \(g(\cdot)\) probability density function corresponding link function \(G(\cdot)\). Partial Effects Discrete Variables: discrete dummy covariate \(x_k\), partial effect calculated discrete difference expected value \(x_k\) changes 0 1, holding variables \(x_{-k}\) constant: $$PE_k(x) = G(x_{-k}\beta_{-k} + \beta_k) - G(x_{-k}\beta_{-k})$$ Average vs. Conditional Partial Effects: - Average Partial Effects (APE): Evaluated observation \(\) sample averaged: $$APE_k = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{=1}^N PE_k(x_i)$$ - Conditional Partial Effects (CPE): Evaluated specific vector covariate values \(x^*\) (e.g., sample mean median): $$CPE_k = PE_k(x^*)$$ calculating standard errors, taken account option previously chosen estimating model. See Ramalho, Ramalho Murteira (2011) Fang Ma (2013) details computation partial effects fractional response framework.
